materials.title: Narrative Reading: Inference and Problem Solving
materials.name: Narrative Reading: Inference and Problem Solving
materials.description: Use a narrative to trace a practical problem, identify evidence, and infer why a temporary solution was revised.

learning_content.what_to_learn: finding explicit information, sequence, inference, and evaluation

materials.text:
When the old footbridge in Suka Jaya became unsafe, the village council planned to close it until a new bridge could be built. The bridge connected the houses on one side of the river with the small health post and market on the other. Most adults could take a longer road, but younger students and older residents depended on the shorter route.

Raka, a seventeen-year-old student, suggested a temporary solution. He noticed that people crossed the bridge most safely in the early evening when a solar lamp near the entrance was working. He asked the council whether several unused lamps from the community hall could be moved closer to the bridge. The council agreed, but only if volunteers checked the path every afternoon.

At first, Raka thought the plan would be easy. On the second day, however, he found that one lamp had been placed where tree branches blocked its light. Instead of blaming the volunteers, he drew a simple map of the bridge and marked the dark areas. The volunteers then moved the lamps and added reflective signs near the weakest part of the path.

A week later, the council still planned to replace the bridge, but it no longer needed to close the route completely. Raka realized that solving a problem did not always mean finding a permanent answer immediately. Sometimes a temporary solution could become useful when people carefully observed what happened and improved it. Residents later used the same approach for other small safety issues: they recorded what they saw, discussed possible causes, and changed one part of the arrangement before judging whether the change worked. This made the process more systematic.

materials.title: Descriptive Reading: Identifying and Organizing Information
materials.name: Descriptive Reading: Identifying and Organizing Information
materials.description: Read a description of a learning facility and practice locating explicit information, organizing details, and inferring user needs.

learning_content.what_to_learn: main idea, supporting details, reference, and organization

materials.text:
The Meranti Learning Library is a small public library beside a senior high school. From the outside, it looks like an ordinary one-storey building, but its interior is arranged for different reading needs. Near the entrance, visitors find a help desk and a shelf containing short books, newspapers, and community notices. This area is usually active because visitors often ask librarians for directions or recommendations.

The middle section contains longer books about science, history, culture, and technology. Tables there are separated enough to allow students to work together without disturbing readers who need quiet. At the back of the building, there is a smaller room with softer lighting. It is used for individual study, online meetings, and students who prefer a quieter environment.

The library also has a digital corner. Four computers are available for research, but users must reserve a session when the room is busy. The librarians do not simply provide books. They also teach visitors how to check whether an online source is reliable.

On Friday afternoons, the library becomes a community learning space. A volunteer may hold a short workshop, while students sometimes help younger children choose books. The library's design reflects one idea: a useful learning space does not have to be large if its areas are planned according to the needs of its users. The librarians also review the arrangement from time to time because the needs of visitors can change. A space that works well for group projects may need different furniture during an examination period. Planning therefore remains an ongoing process.

materials.title: Procedure Reading: Sequencing and Consequences
materials.name: Procedure Reading: Sequencing and Consequences
materials.description: Follow a digital-work procedure and examine sequence, purpose, and consequences when steps are skipped.

learning_content.what_to_learn: purpose, sequence, consequence, and responsible procedure reading

materials.text:
Before a group presentation, students can create a shared folder so that every member can access the latest version of their work. First, one student creates a new folder and gives it a clear name containing the class, project topic, and month. The student then checks the sharing settings and chooses the option that allows group members to edit the files.

Next, the group creates separate subfolders for research, slides, images, and final files. Each member uploads material to the correct location instead of placing everything in the main folder. This makes it easier to find information later.

Before editing a file, members should check whether someone else is already working on it. If two people make major changes to the same document at the same time, important edits may be lost or become difficult to combine. The group can avoid this problem by using comments to suggest changes when direct editing is not necessary.

Finally, the group reviews the folder before the presentation. Old drafts are moved to an archive folder, the final slide deck is checked on another device, and the sharing permission is reviewed once more. These steps take only a few minutes, but they reduce confusion when the presentation day arrives.

materials.title: Recount Reading: Evidence, Assumptions, and Reflection
materials.name: Recount Reading: Evidence, Assumptions, and Reflection
materials.description: Analyze a personal recount by separating observation from assumption and evaluating the lesson drawn from an experience.

learning_content.what_to_learn: fact versus assumption, cause-effect, and reflective interpretation

materials.text:
Last Saturday, our school held a repair workshop with a local community group. The aim was not to teach students how to repair every kind of device, but to show us how careful observation can prevent small problems from becoming expensive ones.

At the beginning, I expected to spend most of the morning watching the instructors. Instead, each group received a broken desk lamp and a checklist. We had to identify visible problems before touching any component. My group noticed that the lamp's switch felt loose, but we did not immediately conclude that the switch was the only problem.

The instructor asked us to describe what we had observed and explain what information we still needed. After checking the cable and plug, we discovered that the loose switch was only part of the problem. A damaged cable was also causing an unstable connection. The instructor used our example to explain why guessing too early can lead to unnecessary repairs.

In the afternoon, we practised writing short repair reports. I found this harder than expected because a useful report had to distinguish observations from assumptions. On the way home, I realized that the most valuable lesson was not a technical trick. It was a way of thinking: inspect first, separate evidence from guesses, and make a decision only after collecting enough information. The instructor emphasized that a repair report should allow another person to understand what was observed, what was tested, and what was concluded. This made the activity relevant beyond the workshop because the same distinction can be useful in other practical situations.

materials.title: Analytical Exposition: Claims, Evidence, and Evaluation
materials.name: Analytical Exposition: Claims, Evidence, and Evaluation
materials.description: Read an analytical exposition and identify claims, evidence, counterarguments, and the writer's qualified conclusion.

learning_content.what_to_learn: claim, evidence, counterargument, relevance, and conclusion

materials.text:
Students encounter information through search engines, social media, videos, and online discussion forums every day. Because information is easy to share, schools should explicitly teach students how to check digital sources rather than assuming that students will develop this skill automatically.

The first reason is that popularity does not prove reliability. A post may receive thousands of views because it is surprising or entertaining, while a careful explanation from a specialist may receive much less attention. Students therefore need to ask who produced the information, what evidence is provided, and whether the claim can be confirmed elsewhere.

A second reason is that online information is often removed from its original context. A photograph may be real but connected to a different event. A quotation may be authentic but presented without the paragraph that explains its meaning. Checking the original source helps students avoid drawing conclusions from incomplete information.

Some people argue that source checking takes too much time for ordinary schoolwork. However, students do not need to investigate every sentence equally. They can focus their effort on claims that influence an important decision, contain surprising statistics, or lack clear evidence.

Teaching source checking would not make students distrust everything online. Instead, it would help them distinguish between information that is merely attractive and information that is sufficiently supported to deserve confidence. Source checking also matters when people share information with friends. A careful student can slow down before forwarding a claim, check its origin, and explain uncertainty instead of presenting an unverified statement as a fact.

materials.title: Descriptive Reading: Connecting Scientific and Community Information
materials.name: Descriptive Reading: Connecting Scientific and Community Information
materials.description: Connect physical description, scientific measurement, and community knowledge to evaluate how information is combined.

learning_content.what_to_learn: integrating measured information with contextual description

materials.text:
The Tanjung Biru Mangrove Learning Center stands at the edge of a coastal village where a narrow river meets the sea. Visitors first see a wooden observation deck built above the mudflats. From the deck, they can observe several mangrove species without walking through the fragile root areas.

The center is divided into three main zones. The first is an outdoor trail used for guided observation. Small signs explain how roots, leaves, and surrounding organisms interact. The second is a simple laboratory where students examine water samples and record changes in salinity. The equipment is basic, but the center emphasizes careful measurement rather than impressive technology.

The third zone is a community room. Fishermen sometimes discuss changes they have noticed along the coast, while students present small research projects. These meetings are useful because scientific measurements and local observations can describe different parts of the same environmental change.

The center does not present the mangrove as a place that must simply be protected from people. Instead, it encourages visitors to understand why certain activities are allowed in some areas and restricted in others. The goal is to make environmental protection practical: people should understand the system well enough to make decisions that reduce damage while keeping the area useful to the community. The center's guides therefore encourage visitors to ask questions about what they observe instead of simply memorizing names of species. The aim is to turn a visit into an opportunity to compare evidence, notice patterns, and think about consequences.

materials.title: Narrative Reading: Audience, Selection, and Purpose
materials.name: Narrative Reading: Audience, Selection, and Purpose
materials.description: Examine how a narrative presents audience, selection of information, and the relationship between research and communication.

learning_content.what_to_learn: audience, selection, clarity, and communicative purpose

materials.text:
Maya was responsible for designing a poster for the school's science exhibition. She had two days left, but the first version looked too crowded. She wanted to include every fact her team had collected because she was afraid that leaving information out would make the project appear incomplete.

Her teammate Dimas suggested that the poster should guide the reader rather than contain the entire research report. Maya disagreed at first. She thought a good poster should show how much work the team had done. Dimas then asked her to stand three steps away and read the poster from that distance. Maya noticed that the headings were difficult to distinguish and that the main finding disappeared among the smaller details.

Instead of deleting information immediately, Maya classified the content into three groups: essential findings, supporting evidence, and details that could be explained during the presentation. The next version was shorter, but it made the main conclusion easier to find.

On exhibition day, a visitor asked about a detail that Maya had removed from the poster. Maya was able to explain it because the team had kept the full report. She realized that simplifying a presentation did not mean reducing the quality of the research. It meant deciding which information the audience needed first and which information could be provided later. After the exhibition, Maya kept both versions of the poster because the difference between them helped her understand the design decision. The experience showed her that revision is not evidence that the original effort was wasted; it is part of communicating research more effectively.

materials.title: Procedure Reading: Responsible Data Collection
materials.name: Procedure Reading: Responsible Data Collection
materials.description: Analyze a survey procedure and evaluate how purpose, question design, sampling, and limitations affect interpretation.

learning_content.what_to_learn: survey purpose, question quality, sampling, and limitations

materials.text:
A short school survey can be useful when students want to understand a problem, but the survey should be planned before questions are distributed. Start by writing one clear purpose, such as finding out which study spaces students use most often. Avoid combining several unrelated purposes in one survey.

Next, write questions that ask for information directly related to the purpose. A question such as “How many days a week do you usually study in the library?” is easier to interpret than a question that asks students to describe their entire study life.

Before sending the survey, test it with a few students who are not part of the main group. Ask them whether any question is confusing or seems to suggest a particular answer. Revise unclear wording before collecting the real responses.

After collecting responses, organize the data before drawing conclusions. Check for unanswered questions and note how many students responded. If only a small group participates, do not automatically claim that the result represents the entire school.

Finally, report the result with its limitations. A responsible survey does not hide inconvenient responses or make a stronger claim than the data support. The purpose of the process is not simply to obtain a number; it is to obtain information that can be interpreted fairly. Students can also explain how the survey was conducted when they present the results. This makes the audience better able to judge whether a conclusion is reasonable and whether the data should be used to guide a wider decision.

materials.title: Recount Reading: Adaptation and Decision Making
materials.name: Recount Reading: Adaptation and Decision Making
materials.description: Follow a travel recount to infer how people adapt plans when new information changes the original situation.

learning_content.what_to_learn: adaptation, route decisions, and evidence-based reflection

materials.text:
During a student exchange trip, our group planned to visit a historical district on the eastern side of the city. We had a map, a meeting time, and a route recommended by the hotel. On the morning of the trip, however, a street festival blocked the road we expected to use.

At first, several students wanted to return to the hotel and wait until the road reopened. Our guide suggested that we first identify which part of the route was actually blocked. We discovered that only the main street was closed. A smaller pedestrian route remained open and connected to a train station.

The alternative route took longer, but it also changed the experience. Instead of passing quickly through the commercial area, we walked through a residential neighborhood and saw a small community museum. The museum was not on our original plan, yet it helped us understand why the district had developed around the old railway.

When we finally reached the historical district, we were twenty minutes late. Our guide did not treat the delay as a failure because the group had communicated its location and adjusted the schedule. That day taught me that a plan is useful when it helps people make decisions, not when everyone follows it without considering new information. Although the original plan was useful, the group benefited from checking reality before deciding what to do next. The experience made the narrator more comfortable with changing a plan without treating the change as evidence that the original planning had been pointless.

materials.title: Analytical Exposition: Comparing Learning Formats
materials.name: Analytical Exposition: Comparing Learning Formats
materials.description: Evaluate an argument about printed and digital learning resources by comparing evidence and recognizing a balanced position.

learning_content.what_to_learn: balanced comparison, access, and purpose-based resource choice

materials.text:
Digital resources have changed the way students study. A single device can store thousands of pages, provide search tools, and make it possible to update information quickly. Even so, schools should keep some printed resources instead of replacing every book with a digital version.

One reason is access. Not every student has the same device quality, battery life, or internet connection outside school. A printed reference book can be used without charging a battery or depending on a network. Keeping a small collection of essential materials can therefore reduce the effect of unequal access.

Printed resources can also support certain study habits. Some students find it easier to annotate a page, compare two pages at once, or read without notifications. This does not mean printed books are always better. Digital tools are valuable when students need search functions, multimedia explanations, or frequently updated information.

The strongest approach is therefore not to choose one format for every purpose. Schools can use digital resources where their advantages are clear and maintain printed materials where they provide reliable access or support focused reading.

Replacing every printed resource may appear efficient because it reduces physical storage. However, efficiency should be measured by how well students can actually use the resources, not only by how little space they occupy. This balanced position also leaves room for schools to reconsider their mix of resources as students' needs and technologies change. The writer's point is therefore about choosing tools deliberately rather than defending one format regardless of purpose.

materials.title: Descriptive Reading: Information, Accessibility, and Coordination
materials.name: Descriptive Reading: Information, Accessibility, and Coordination
materials.description: Read a public-facility description and connect information design, accessibility, and community coordination.

learning_content.what_to_learn: information clarity, accessibility, coordination, and user needs

materials.text:
The Cempaka Mobility Hub is a small public facility built near a bus stop and a bicycle lane. Its purpose is to make short transfers between different forms of transportation easier. The hub contains a covered waiting area, bicycle parking, a drinking-water station, and a digital board showing departure information.

The most noticeable feature is the information board. Instead of displaying only bus times, it shows whether a service is delayed and identifies the nearest alternative route. A smaller panel provides walking directions to nearby public facilities. The information is updated by the transport operator, while the local community group reports problems such as damaged signs or blocked paths.

The hub was designed with different users in mind. A ramp connects the waiting area to the sidewalk, and seats are placed at different heights. Bicycle users can park close to the lane without blocking the pedestrian path.

The facility is not a large transportation terminal. It handles only a small number of passengers at one time. Its value comes from coordination: several simple services are placed together so that users can move between them with less confusion. The local council evaluates the hub not only by how many people use it, but also by whether the information is clear and whether the facility remains accessible to different users. The hub's design also makes small problems visible to the people responsible for maintaining the area. In that sense, the facility is not only a place to wait; it is a point where information about movement and access can be shared between users and service providers.

topics.title: Descriptive Reading: Connecting Scientific and Community Information
topics.name: Descriptive Reading: Connecting Scientific and Community Information
topics.description: Connect physical description, scientific measurement, and community knowledge to evaluate how information is combined.

learning_content.what_to_learn: integrating measured information with contextual description

topics.text:
The Tanjung Biru Mangrove Learning Center stands at the edge of a coastal village where a narrow river meets the sea. Visitors first see a wooden observation deck built above the mudflats. From the deck, they can observe several mangrove species without walking through the fragile root areas.

The center is divided into three main zones. The first is an outdoor trail used for guided observation. Small signs explain how roots, leaves, and surrounding organisms interact. The second is a simple laboratory where students examine water samples and record changes in salinity. The equipment is basic, but the center emphasizes careful measurement rather than impressive technology.

The third zone is a community room. Fishermen sometimes discuss changes they have noticed along the coast, while students present small research projects. These meetings are useful because scientific measurements and local observations can describe different parts of the same environmental change.

The center does not present the mangrove as a place that must simply be protected from people. Instead, it encourages visitors to understand why certain activities are allowed in some areas and restricted in others. The goal is to make environmental protection practical: people should understand the system well enough to make decisions that reduce damage while keeping the area useful to the community. The center's guides therefore encourage visitors to ask questions about what they observe instead of simply memorizing names of species. The aim is to turn a visit into an opportunity to compare evidence, notice patterns, and think about consequences.

topics.title: Narrative Reading: Audience, Selection, and Purpose
topics.name: Narrative Reading: Audience, Selection, and Purpose
topics.description: Examine how a narrative presents audience, selection of information, and the relationship between research and communication.

learning_content.what_to_learn: audience, selection, clarity, and communicative purpose

topics.text:
Maya was responsible for designing a poster for the school's science exhibition. She had two days left, but the first version looked too crowded. She wanted to include every fact her team had collected because she was afraid that leaving information out would make the project appear incomplete.

Her teammate Dimas suggested that the poster should guide the reader rather than contain the entire research report. Maya disagreed at first. She thought a good poster should show how much work the team had done. Dimas then asked her to stand three steps away and read the poster from that distance. Maya noticed that the headings were difficult to distinguish and that the main finding disappeared among the smaller details.

Instead of deleting information immediately, Maya classified the content into three groups: essential findings, supporting evidence, and details that could be explained during the presentation. The next version was shorter, but it made the main conclusion easier to find.

On exhibition day, a visitor asked about a detail that Maya had removed from the poster. Maya was able to explain it because the team had kept the full report. She realized that simplifying a presentation did not mean reducing the quality of the research. It meant deciding which information the audience needed first and which information could be provided later. After the exhibition, Maya kept both versions of the poster because the difference between them helped her understand the design decision. The experience showed her that revision is not evidence that the original effort was wasted; it is part of communicating research more effectively.

topics.title: Procedure Reading: Responsible Data Collection
topics.name: Procedure Reading: Responsible Data Collection
topics.description: Analyze a survey procedure and evaluate how purpose, question design, sampling, and limitations affect interpretation.

learning_content.what_to_learn: survey purpose, question quality, sampling, and limitations

topics.text:
A short school survey can be useful when students want to understand a problem, but the survey should be planned before questions are distributed. Start by writing one clear purpose, such as finding out which study spaces students use most often. Avoid combining several unrelated purposes in one survey.

Next, write questions that ask for information directly related to the purpose. A question such as “How many days a week do you usually study in the library?” is easier to interpret than a question that asks students to describe their entire study life.

Before sending the survey, test it with a few students who are not part of the main group. Ask them whether any question is confusing or seems to suggest a particular answer. Revise unclear wording before collecting the real responses.

After collecting responses, organize the data before drawing conclusions. Check for unanswered questions and note how many students responded. If only a small group participates, do not automatically claim that the result represents the entire school.

Finally, report the result with its limitations. A responsible survey does not hide inconvenient responses or make a stronger claim than the data support. The purpose of the process is not simply to obtain a number; it is to obtain information that can be interpreted fairly. Students can also explain how the survey was conducted when they present the results. This makes the audience better able to judge whether a conclusion is reasonable and whether the data should be used to guide a wider decision.

topics.title: Recount Reading: Adaptation and Decision Making
topics.name: Recount Reading: Adaptation and Decision Making
topics.description: Follow a travel recount to infer how people adapt plans when new information changes the original situation.

learning_content.what_to_learn: adaptation, route decisions, and evidence-based reflection

topics.text:
During a student exchange trip, our group planned to visit a historical district on the eastern side of the city. We had a map, a meeting time, and a route recommended by the hotel. On the morning of the trip, however, a street festival blocked the road we expected to use.

At first, several students wanted to return to the hotel and wait until the road reopened. Our guide suggested that we first identify which part of the route was actually blocked. We discovered that only the main street was closed. A smaller pedestrian route remained open and connected to a train station.

The alternative route took longer, but it also changed the experience. Instead of passing quickly through the commercial area, we walked through a residential neighborhood and saw a small community museum. The museum was not on our original plan, yet it helped us understand why the district had developed around the old railway.

When we finally reached the historical district, we were twenty minutes late. Our guide did not treat the delay as a failure because the group had communicated its location and adjusted the schedule. That day taught me that a plan is useful when it helps people make decisions, not when everyone follows it without considering new information. Although the original plan was useful, the group benefited from checking reality before deciding what to do next. The experience made the narrator more comfortable with changing a plan without treating the change as evidence that the original planning had been pointless.

topics.title: Analytical Exposition: Comparing Learning Formats
topics.name: Analytical Exposition: Comparing Learning Formats
topics.description: Evaluate an argument about printed and digital learning resources by comparing evidence and recognizing a balanced position.

learning_content.what_to_learn: balanced comparison, access, and purpose-based resource choice

topics.text:
Digital resources have changed the way students study. A single device can store thousands of pages, provide search tools, and make it possible to update information quickly. Even so, schools should keep some printed resources instead of replacing every book with a digital version.

One reason is access. Not every student has the same device quality, battery life, or internet connection outside school. A printed reference book can be used without charging a battery or depending on a network. Keeping a small collection of essential materials can therefore reduce the effect of unequal access.

Printed resources can also support certain study habits. Some students find it easier to annotate a page, compare two pages at once, or read without notifications. This does not mean printed books are always better. Digital tools are valuable when students need search functions, multimedia explanations, or frequently updated information.

The strongest approach is therefore not to choose one format for every purpose. Schools can use digital resources where their advantages are clear and maintain printed materials where they provide reliable access or support focused reading.

Replacing every printed resource may appear efficient because it reduces physical storage. However, efficiency should be measured by how well students can actually use the resources, not only by how little space they occupy. This balanced position also leaves room for schools to reconsider their mix of resources as students' needs and technologies change. The writer's point is therefore about choosing tools deliberately rather than defending one format regardless of purpose.

topics.title: Descriptive Reading: Information, Accessibility, and Coordination
topics.name: Descriptive Reading: Information, Accessibility, and Coordination
topics.description: Read a public-facility description and connect information design, accessibility, and community coordination.

learning_content.what_to_learn: information clarity, accessibility, coordination, and user needs

topics.text:
The Cempaka Mobility Hub is a small public facility built near a bus stop and a bicycle lane. Its purpose is to make short transfers between different forms of transportation easier. The hub contains a covered waiting area, bicycle parking, a drinking-water station, and a digital board showing departure information.

The most noticeable feature is the information board. Instead of displaying only bus times, it shows whether a service is delayed and identifies the nearest alternative route. A smaller panel provides walking directions to nearby public facilities. The information is updated by the transport operator, while the local community group reports problems such as damaged signs or blocked paths.

The hub was designed with different users in mind. A ramp connects the waiting area to the sidewalk, and seats are placed at different heights. Bicycle users can park close to the lane without blocking the pedestrian path.

The facility is not a large transportation terminal. It handles only a small number of passengers at one time. Its value comes from coordination: several simple services are placed together so that users can move between them with less confusion. The local council evaluates the hub not only by how many people use it, but also by whether the information is clear and whether the facility remains accessible to different users. The hub's design also makes small problems visible to the people responsible for maintaining the area. In that sense, the facility is not only a place to wait; it is a point where information about movement and access can be shared between users and service providers.

question_bank.stimulus:
When the old footbridge in Suka Jaya became unsafe, the village council planned to close it until a new bridge could be built. The bridge connected the houses on one side of the river with the small health post and market on the other. Most adults could take a longer road, but younger students and older residents depended on the shorter route.

Raka, a seventeen-year-old student, suggested a temporary solution. He noticed that people crossed the bridge most safely in the early evening when a solar lamp near the entrance was working. He asked the council whether several unused lamps from the community hall could be moved closer to the bridge. The council agreed, but only if volunteers checked the path every afternoon.

At first, Raka thought the plan would be easy. On the second day, however, he found that one lamp had been placed where tree branches blocked its light. Instead of blaming the volunteers, he drew a simple map of the bridge and marked the dark areas. The volunteers then moved the lamps and added reflective signs near the weakest part of the path.

A week later, the council still planned to replace the bridge, but it no longer needed to close the route completely. Raka realized that solving a problem did not always mean finding a permanent answer immediately. Sometimes a temporary solution could become useful when people carefully observed what happened and improved it. Residents later used the same approach for other small safety issues: they recorded what they saw, discussed possible causes, and changed one part of the arrangement before judging whether the change worked. This made the process more systematic.

question_bank.stimulus:
Last Saturday, our school held a repair workshop with a local community group. The aim was not to teach students how to repair every kind of device, but to show us how careful observation can prevent small problems from becoming expensive ones.

At the beginning, I expected to spend most of the morning watching the instructors. Instead, each group received a broken desk lamp and a checklist. We had to identify visible problems before touching any component. My group noticed that the lamp's switch felt loose, but we did not immediately conclude that the switch was the only problem.

The instructor asked us to describe what we had observed and explain what information we still needed. After checking the cable and plug, we discovered that the loose switch was only part of the problem. A damaged cable was also causing an unstable connection. The instructor used our example to explain why guessing too early can lead to unnecessary repairs.

The instructor emphasized that a repair report should allow another person to understand what was observed, what was tested, and what was concluded. This made the activity relevant beyond the workshop because the same distinction can be useful in other practical situations.

question_bank.stimulus:
Last Saturday, our school held a repair workshop with a local community group. The aim was not to teach students how to repair every kind of device, but to show us how careful observation can prevent small problems from becoming expensive ones.

At the beginning, I expected to spend most of the morning watching the instructors. Instead, each group received a broken desk lamp and a checklist. We had to identify visible problems before touching any component. My group noticed that the lamp's switch felt loose, but we did not immediately conclude that the switch was the only problem.

The instructor asked us to describe what we had observed and explain what information we still needed. After checking the cable and plug, we discovered that the loose switch was only part of the problem. A damaged cable was also causing an unstable connection. The instructor used our example to explain why guessing too early can lead to unnecessary repairs.

In the afternoon, we practised writing short repair reports. I found this harder than expected because a useful report had to distinguish observations from assumptions. On the way home, I realized that the most valuable lesson was not a technical trick. It was a way of thinking: inspect first, separate evidence from guesses, and make a decision only after collecting enough information. The instructor emphasized that a repair report should allow another person to understand what was observed, what was tested, and what was concluded. This made the activity relevant beyond the workshop because the same distinction can be useful in other practical situations.

question_bank.stimulus:
Students encounter information through search engines, social media, videos, and online discussion forums every day. Because information is easy to share, schools should explicitly teach students how to check digital sources rather than assuming that students will develop this skill automatically.

The first reason is that popularity does not prove reliability. A post may receive thousands of views because it is surprising or entertaining, while a careful explanation from a specialist may receive much less attention. Students therefore need to ask who produced the information, what evidence is provided, and whether the claim can be confirmed elsewhere.

A second reason is that online information is often removed from its original context. A photograph may be real but connected to a different event. A quotation may be authentic but presented without the paragraph that explains its meaning. Checking the original source helps students avoid drawing conclusions from incomplete information.

Some people argue that source checking takes too much time for ordinary schoolwork. However, students do not need to investigate every sentence equally. They can focus their effort on claims that influence an important decision, contain surprising statistics, or lack clear evidence.

Teaching source checking would not make students distrust everything online. Instead, it would help them distinguish between information that is merely attractive and information that is sufficiently supported to deserve confidence. Source checking also matters when people share information with friends. A careful student can slow down before forwarding a claim, check its origin, and explain uncertainty instead of presenting an unverified statement as a fact.

question_bank.stimulus:
A short school survey can be useful when students want to understand a problem, but the survey should be planned before questions are distributed. Start by writing one clear purpose, such as finding out which study spaces students use most often. Avoid combining several unrelated purposes in one survey.

Next, write questions that ask for information directly related to the purpose. A question such as “How many days a week do you usually study in the library?” is easier to interpret than a question that asks students to describe their entire study life.

Before sending the survey, test it with a few students who are not part of the main group. Ask them whether any question is confusing or seems to suggest a particular answer. Revise unclear wording before collecting the real responses.

After collecting responses, organize the data before drawing conclusions. Check for unanswered questions and note how many students responded. If only a small group participates, do not automatically claim that the result represents the entire school.

Finally, report the result with its limitations. A responsible survey does not hide inconvenient responses or make a stronger claim than the data support. The purpose of the process is not simply to obtain a number; it is to obtain information that can be interpreted fairly. Students can also explain how the survey was conducted when they present the results. This makes the audience better able to judge whether a conclusion is reasonable and whether the data should be used to guide a wider decision.

question_bank.stimulus:
Digital resources have changed the way students study. A single device can store thousands of pages, provide search tools, and make it possible to update information quickly. Even so, schools should keep some printed resources instead of replacing every book with a digital version.

One reason is access. Not every student has the same device quality, battery life, or internet connection outside school. A printed reference book can be used without charging a battery or depending on a network. Keeping a small collection of essential materials can therefore reduce the effect of unequal access.

Printed resources can also support certain study habits. Some students find it easier to annotate a page, compare two pages at once, or read without notifications. This does not mean printed books are always better. Digital tools are valuable when students need search functions, multimedia explanations, or frequently updated information.

The strongest approach is therefore not to choose one format for every purpose. Schools can use digital resources where their advantages are clear and maintain printed materials where they provide reliable access or support focused reading.

Replacing every printed resource may appear efficient because it reduces physical storage. However, efficiency should be measured by how well students can actually use the resources, not only by how little space they occupy. This balanced position also leaves room for schools to reconsider their mix of resources as students' needs and technologies change. The writer's point is therefore about choosing tools deliberately rather than defending one format regardless of purpose.

question_bank.stimulus:
The Cempaka Mobility Hub is a small public facility built near a bus stop and a bicycle lane. Its purpose is to make short transfers between different forms of transportation easier. The hub contains a covered waiting area, bicycle parking, a drinking-water station, and a digital board showing departure information.

The most noticeable feature is the information board. Instead of displaying only bus times, it shows whether a service is delayed and identifies the nearest alternative route. A smaller panel provides walking directions to nearby public facilities. The information is updated by the transport operator, while the local community group reports problems such as damaged signs or blocked paths.

The hub was designed with different users in mind. A ramp connects the waiting area to the sidewalk, and seats are placed at different heights. Bicycle users can park close to the lane without blocking the pedestrian path.

The facility is not a large transportation terminal. It handles only a small number of passengers at one time. Its value comes from coordination: several simple services are placed together so that users can move between them with less confusion. The local council evaluates the hub not only by how many people use it, but also by whether the information is clear and whether the facility remains accessible to different users. The hub's design also makes small problems visible to the people responsible for maintaining the area. In that sense, the facility is not only a place to wait; it is a point where information about movement and access can be shared between users and service providers.

stimuli.title: The Lantern at the River
stimuli.text:
When the old footbridge in Suka Jaya became unsafe, the village council planned to close it until a new bridge could be built. The bridge connected the houses on one side of the river with the small health post and market on the other. Most adults could take a longer road, but younger students and older residents depended on the shorter route.

Raka, a seventeen-year-old student, suggested a temporary solution. He noticed that people crossed the bridge most safely in the early evening when a solar lamp near the entrance was working. He asked the council whether several unused lamps from the community hall could be moved closer to the bridge. The council agreed, but only if volunteers checked the path every afternoon.

At first, Raka thought the plan would be easy. On the second day, however, he found that one lamp had been placed where tree branches blocked its light. Instead of blaming the volunteers, he drew a simple map of the bridge and marked the dark areas. The volunteers then moved the lamps and added reflective signs near the weakest part of the path.

A week later, the council still planned to replace the bridge, but it no longer needed to close the route completely. Raka realized that solving a problem did not always mean finding a permanent answer immediately. Sometimes a temporary solution could become useful when people carefully observed what happened and improved it. Residents later used the same approach for other small safety issues: they recorded what they saw, discussed possible causes, and changed one part of the arrangement before judging whether the change worked. This made the process more systematic.

stimuli.title: A Library Designed for Different Readers
stimuli.text:
The Meranti Learning Library is a small public library beside a senior high school. From the outside, it looks like an ordinary one-storey building, but its interior is arranged for different reading needs. Near the entrance, visitors find a help desk and a shelf containing short books, newspapers, and community notices. This area is usually active because visitors often ask librarians for directions or recommendations.

The middle section contains longer books about science, history, culture, and technology. Tables there are separated enough to allow students to work together without disturbing readers who need quiet. At the back of the building, there is a smaller room with softer lighting. It is used for individual study, online meetings, and students who prefer a quieter environment.

The library also has a digital corner. Four computers are available for research, but users must reserve a session when the room is busy. The librarians do not simply provide books. They also teach visitors how to check whether an online source is reliable.

On Friday afternoons, the library becomes a community learning space. A volunteer may hold a short workshop, while students sometimes help younger children choose books. The library's design reflects one idea: a useful learning space does not have to be large if its areas are planned according to the needs of its users. The librarians also review the arrangement from time to time because the needs of visitors can change. A space that works well for group projects may need different furniture during an examination period. Planning therefore remains an ongoing process.

stimuli.title: Preparing a Shared Presentation Folder
stimuli.text:
Before a group presentation, students can create a shared folder so that every member can access the latest version of their work. First, one student creates a new folder and gives it a clear name containing the class, project topic, and month. The student then checks the sharing settings and chooses the option that allows group members to edit the files.

Next, the group creates separate subfolders for research, slides, images, and final files. Each member uploads material to the correct location instead of placing everything in the main folder. This makes it easier to find information later.

Before editing a file, members should check whether someone else is already working on it. If two people make major changes to the same document at the same time, important edits may be lost or become difficult to combine. The group can avoid this problem by using comments to suggest changes when direct editing is not necessary.

Finally, the group reviews the folder before the presentation. Old drafts are moved to an archive folder, the final slide deck is checked on another device, and the sharing permission is reviewed once more. These steps take only a few minutes, but they reduce confusion when the presentation day arrives.

stimuli.title: The Saturday Repair Workshop
stimuli.text:
Last Saturday, our school held a repair workshop with a local community group. The aim was not to teach students how to repair every kind of device, but to show us how careful observation can prevent small problems from becoming expensive ones.

At the beginning, I expected to spend most of the morning watching the instructors. Instead, each group received a broken desk lamp and a checklist. We had to identify visible problems before touching any component. My group noticed that the lamp's switch felt loose, but we did not immediately conclude that the switch was the only problem.

The instructor asked us to describe what we had observed and explain what information we still needed. After checking the cable and plug, we discovered that the loose switch was only part of the problem. A damaged cable was also causing an unstable connection. The instructor used our example to explain why guessing too early can lead to unnecessary repairs.

In the afternoon, we practised writing short repair reports. I found this harder than expected because a useful report had to distinguish observations from assumptions. On the way home, I realized that the most valuable lesson was not a technical trick. It was a way of thinking: inspect first, separate evidence from guesses, and make a decision only after collecting enough information. The instructor emphasized that a repair report should allow another person to understand what was observed, what was tested, and what was concluded. This made the activity relevant beyond the workshop because the same distinction can be useful in other practical situations.

stimuli.title: Why Schools Should Teach Digital Source Checking
stimuli.text:
Students encounter information through search engines, social media, videos, and online discussion forums every day. Because information is easy to share, schools should explicitly teach students how to check digital sources rather than assuming that students will develop this skill automatically.

The first reason is that popularity does not prove reliability. A post may receive thousands of views because it is surprising or entertaining, while a careful explanation from a specialist may receive much less attention. Students therefore need to ask who produced the information, what evidence is provided, and whether the claim can be confirmed elsewhere.

A second reason is that online information is often removed from its original context. A photograph may be real but connected to a different event. A quotation may be authentic but presented without the paragraph that explains its meaning. Checking the original source helps students avoid drawing conclusions from incomplete information.

Some people argue that source checking takes too much time for ordinary schoolwork. However, students do not need to investigate every sentence equally. They can focus their effort on claims that influence an important decision, contain surprising statistics, or lack clear evidence.

Teaching source checking would not make students distrust everything online. Instead, it would help them distinguish between information that is merely attractive and information that is sufficiently supported to deserve confidence. Source checking also matters when people share information with friends. A careful student can slow down before forwarding a claim, check its origin, and explain uncertainty instead of presenting an unverified statement as a fact.

stimuli.title: A Coastal Mangrove Learning Center
stimuli.text:
The Tanjung Biru Mangrove Learning Center stands at the edge of a coastal village where a narrow river meets the sea. Visitors first see a wooden observation deck built above the mudflats. From the deck, they can observe several mangrove species without walking through the fragile root areas.

The center is divided into three main zones. The first is an outdoor trail used for guided observation. Small signs explain how roots, leaves, and surrounding organisms interact. The second is a simple laboratory where students examine water samples and record changes in salinity. The equipment is basic, but the center emphasizes careful measurement rather than impressive technology.

The third zone is a community room. Fishermen sometimes discuss changes they have noticed along the coast, while students present small research projects. These meetings are useful because scientific measurements and local observations can describe different parts of the same environmental change.

The center does not present the mangrove as a place that must simply be protected from people. Instead, it encourages visitors to understand why certain activities are allowed in some areas and restricted in others. The goal is to make environmental protection practical: people should understand the system well enough to make decisions that reduce damage while keeping the area useful to the community. The center's guides therefore encourage visitors to ask questions about what they observe instead of simply memorizing names of species. The aim is to turn a visit into an opportunity to compare evidence, notice patterns, and think about consequences.

stimuli.title: The Unfinished Poster
stimuli.text:
Maya was responsible for designing a poster for the school's science exhibition. She had two days left, but the first version looked too crowded. She wanted to include every fact her team had collected because she was afraid that leaving information out would make the project appear incomplete.

Her teammate Dimas suggested that the poster should guide the reader rather than contain the entire research report. Maya disagreed at first. She thought a good poster should show how much work the team had done. Dimas then asked her to stand three steps away and read the poster from that distance. Maya noticed that the headings were difficult to distinguish and that the main finding disappeared among the smaller details.

Instead of deleting information immediately, Maya classified the content into three groups: essential findings, supporting evidence, and details that could be explained during the presentation. The next version was shorter, but it made the main conclusion easier to find.

On exhibition day, a visitor asked about a detail that Maya had removed from the poster. Maya was able to explain it because the team had kept the full report. She realized that simplifying a presentation did not mean reducing the quality of the research. It meant deciding which information the audience needed first and which information could be provided later. After the exhibition, Maya kept both versions of the poster because the difference between them helped her understand the design decision. The experience showed her that revision is not evidence that the original effort was wasted; it is part of communicating research more effectively.

stimuli.title: Using a School Survey Responsibly
stimuli.text:
A short school survey can be useful when students want to understand a problem, but the survey should be planned before questions are distributed. Start by writing one clear purpose, such as finding out which study spaces students use most often. Avoid combining several unrelated purposes in one survey.

Next, write questions that ask for information directly related to the purpose. A question such as “How many days a week do you usually study in the library?” is easier to interpret than a question that asks students to describe their entire study life.

Before sending the survey, test it with a few students who are not part of the main group. Ask them whether any question is confusing or seems to suggest a particular answer. Revise unclear wording before collecting the real responses.

After collecting responses, organize the data before drawing conclusions. Check for unanswered questions and note how many students responded. If only a small group participates, do not automatically claim that the result represents the entire school.

Finally, report the result with its limitations. A responsible survey does not hide inconvenient responses or make a stronger claim than the data support. The purpose of the process is not simply to obtain a number; it is to obtain information that can be interpreted fairly. Students can also explain how the survey was conducted when they present the results. This makes the audience better able to judge whether a conclusion is reasonable and whether the data should be used to guide a wider decision.

stimuli.title: A Day Without the Usual Route
stimuli.text:
During a student exchange trip, our group planned to visit a historical district on the eastern side of the city. We had a map, a meeting time, and a route recommended by the hotel. On the morning of the trip, however, a street festival blocked the road we expected to use.

At first, several students wanted to return to the hotel and wait until the road reopened. Our guide suggested that we first identify which part of the route was actually blocked. We discovered that only the main street was closed. A smaller pedestrian route remained open and connected to a train station.

The alternative route took longer, but it also changed the experience. Instead of passing quickly through the commercial area, we walked through a residential neighborhood and saw a small community museum. The museum was not on our original plan, yet it helped us understand why the district had developed around the old railway.

When we finally reached the historical district, we were twenty minutes late. Our guide did not treat the delay as a failure because the group had communicated its location and adjusted the schedule. That day taught me that a plan is useful when it helps people make decisions, not when everyone follows it without considering new information. Although the original plan was useful, the group benefited from checking reality before deciding what to do next. The experience made the narrator more comfortable with changing a plan without treating the change as evidence that the original planning had been pointless.

stimuli.title: Should Schools Keep Some Printed Resources?
stimuli.text:
Digital resources have changed the way students study. A single device can store thousands of pages, provide search tools, and make it possible to update information quickly. Even so, schools should keep some printed resources instead of replacing every book with a digital version.

One reason is access. Not every student has the same device quality, battery life, or internet connection outside school. A printed reference book can be used without charging a battery or depending on a network. Keeping a small collection of essential materials can therefore reduce the effect of unequal access.

Printed resources can also support certain study habits. Some students find it easier to annotate a page, compare two pages at once, or read without notifications. This does not mean printed books are always better. Digital tools are valuable when students need search functions, multimedia explanations, or frequently updated information.

The strongest approach is therefore not to choose one format for every purpose. Schools can use digital resources where their advantages are clear and maintain printed materials where they provide reliable access or support focused reading.

Replacing every printed resource may appear efficient because it reduces physical storage. However, efficiency should be measured by how well students can actually use the resources, not only by how little space they occupy. This balanced position also leaves room for schools to reconsider their mix of resources as students' needs and technologies change. The writer's point is therefore about choosing tools deliberately rather than defending one format regardless of purpose.

stimuli.title: The Community Mobility Hub
stimuli.text:
The Cempaka Mobility Hub is a small public facility built near a bus stop and a bicycle lane. Its purpose is to make short transfers between different forms of transportation easier. The hub contains a covered waiting area, bicycle parking, a drinking-water station, and a digital board showing departure information.

The most noticeable feature is the information board. Instead of displaying only bus times, it shows whether a service is delayed and identifies the nearest alternative route. A smaller panel provides walking directions to nearby public facilities. The information is updated by the transport operator, while the local community group reports problems such as damaged signs or blocked paths.

The hub was designed with different users in mind. A ramp connects the waiting area to the sidewalk, and seats are placed at different heights. Bicycle users can park close to the lane without blocking the pedestrian path.

The facility is not a large transportation terminal. It handles only a small number of passengers at one time. Its value comes from coordination: several simple services are placed together so that users can move between them with less confusion. The local council evaluates the hub not only by how many people use it, but also by whether the information is clear and whether the facility remains accessible to different users. The hub's design also makes small problems visible to the people responsible for maintaining the area. In that sense, the facility is not only a place to wait; it is a point where information about movement and access can be shared between users and service providers.
